title: Returning to Chicago in 1928; what made the Chicago style
summary: Ashcraft says a definable Chicago style existed, driven by repeated notes and rhythmic force as in Freeman and Muggsy.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: When did you return to Chicago, uh, and, and become acquainted with the picture in Chicago again? Was that six, seven, eight years later, or?
Yeah. Well, by 28, there was a pretty well-established Chicago style, was there? Uh, anybody from Chicago would be recognized if he strayed, uh, a couple hundred miles away.

Connon denies that, of course. But I think that's just because Connon doesn't like tags on anything. Uh. Uh, to me there always has been. I think it's as definable as, let's say, Kansas City, certainly.
If not. Uh, still, there was a little crossing here. For example, Wingy's bands might be called Chicago bands. And with Wingy leading them, they were New Orleans bands.

But he had a great affection for the Chicago musicians. And, uh, so there, there, there are the two things. There are, there is the pure Chicago and there's the misogynist Chicago. And, and, uh, through it all, why, there's a tendency to be able to classify, uh, the Chicago groups as, strictly as Chicago.

There was something, a lot had to do with drive. And, uh, you, you find that in, in, uh, musicians that play the same note a lot, like Muggsy. And, uh, I think Bud, they used to call one note Freeman at one point. And that's partly because he didn't know many other notes. But a lot of it was because he was just banging one note. And he'd keep at it. And it was.
They were after a maximum rhythmic effect.
Out of, uh, whether it's melody or what it was. Get a maximum rhythmic effect.
